Key Research Thinking Patterns: Comparative Analysis: Systematically analyzing differences and similarities between distinct biological groups. (e.g., Comparing the cognitive-behavioral profiles of fish species with different mating systems (coercive vs. mixed-tactic) or examining how F1 hybrids differ in life-history traits from their parental cave and surface-dwelling ecotypes).

Environmental Standardization: Using controlled experimental setups to minimize environmental variation and isolate the effects of genetics or specific treatments. (e.g., Raising fish from different geographic populations or ecotypes in "common-garden" conditions or "ecologically identical mesocosms" to ensure that observed differences in traits are heritable and not just a result of their original environments).

Theory-Driven Experimentation: Designing studies to explicitly test predictions derived from established biological or evolutionary theories. (e.g., Testing the prediction that females from more socially complex (mixed-tactic) mating systems will exhibit greater cognitive flexibility, or that F1 hybrids will have lower fitness (postzygotic isolation) than parental ecotypes).

Integrative Biological Analysis: Connecting phenomena across multiple biological levels, from large-scale evolutionary patterns to fine-scale organismal mechanisms. (e.g., Linking an evolutionary pattern (speciation in caves) to organism-level traits (life-history) and then investigating the underlying genetic mechanism (sex-specific opposing dominance in hybrids))
Summary Description: Dr. Ingo Schlupp specializes in Behavioral Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, exploring their interplay with Speciation Research and Animal Cognition. His research primarily utilizes livebearing fishes (Poeciliidae), including Poecilia and Limia. He investigates hybridization, focusing on hybrid fitness, postzygotic isolation, and the origin of unisexual species like the Amazon molly, Poecilia formosa. He applies common-garden experiments, behavioral assays, and cognitive profiling to study mate choice, mating tactics, life-history evolution, and animal welfare. Significant contributions include identifying sex-specific (opposing) dominance in hybrid trait expression and linking male mating tactics (coercion vs. courtship) to distinct female cognitive-behavioral profiles.
